newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austria insurer says to pay out holocaust claims.
newsitem.headline: Austria insurer says to pay out holocaust claims.

text.p: Leading Austrian insurer Wiener Allianz Versicherungs AG responded to a U.S. lawsuit by holocaust victims and their families on Thursday with a promise to reimburse genuine claims.

Wiener Allianz, part of Germany's Allianz group, and fellow Vienna firm Der Anker Allgemeine Versicherung AG are among seven European companies facing a billion dollar damages suit for allegedly withholding the proceeds of policies sold between 1920 and 1945.
"Of course we will satisfy anyone who comes to us with a real claim," Wiener Allianz spokeswoman Marita Roloff said.
She added the firm had yet to receive formal notification of the lawsuit, filed in Manhattan federal court on Monday, but was already undertaking its own research.
"We have found that a 67-year-old woman living in the United States has made a claim based on one or more insurance policies she says were taken out by her father in 1929 and 1930," Roloff said.
The woman claimed she had first approached Wiener Allianz soon after the end of World War Two, Roloff said. The policies were apparently with Oesterreichische Phoenix, renamed Wiener Allianz in 1938.

Der Anker Versicherungs AG, a unit of Swiss Helvetia, has remained silent on the matter so far, noting only that crucial records went up in smoke in 1945 when allied bombs destroyed its Vienna headquarters.
Austria, annexed by Nazi Germany in 1938, fought alongside Adolf Hitler's troops in World War Two.
The U.S. lawsuit seeks class action certification and estimates the number of plaintiffs could exceed 10,000.

It claims that seven Austrian, German, French and Italian insurance firms encouraged European citizens fearful of Nazi persecution to deposit their assets and purchase policies to safeguard their families' futures.
Those class members who were unable to flee persecution were arrested and their assets, including the insurance policies, were taken by the Nazis, the suit alleged.
Austrian Jewish leaders called on the insurance companies to respond quickly to the charges.

"In the Swiss banks we have an excellent example of how not to behave in the first few weeks and a good example of how to behave subsequently in the setting up of a holocaust fund," said cultural community president Paul Grosz.
"The aim should be to help the victims and those left behind while cathartically cleansing oneself of guilt by accepting that guilt exists," he continued.
Veteran Nazi hunter Simon Wiesenthal urged the firms to be "generous" rather than "small-minded" in the search for a solution.
